title: Scaling Reasoning can Improve Factuality inLarge Language Models
authors: Mike Zhang              Johannes Bjerva              Russa BiswasDepartment of Computer ScienceAalborg UniversityCopenhagen, Denmark{jjz, jbjerva, rubi}@cs.aau.dk
abstract:
AbstractRecent studies on large language model (LLM) reasoning capabilities have demonstrated promising improvements in model performance by leveraging a lengthythinkingprocess and additional computational resources during inference, primarily in tasks involving mathematical reasoningMuennighoff et al. (2025). However, it remains uncertain if longer reasoning chains inherently enhance factual accuracy, particularly beyond mathematical contexts. In this work, we thoroughly examine LLM reasoning within complex open-domain question-answering (QA) scenarios. We initially distill reasoning traces from advanced, large-scale reasoning models (QwQ-32BandDeepSeek-R1-671B), then fine-tune a variety of models ranging from smaller, instruction-tuned variants to larger architectures based onQwen2.5. To enrich reasoning traces, we introduce factual information from knowledge graphs in the form of paths into our reasoning traces. Our experimental setup includes four baseline approaches and six different instruction-tuned models evaluated across a benchmark of six datasets, encompassing over 22.6K questions. Overall, we carry out 168 experimental runs and analyze approximately 1.7 million reasoning traces. Our findings indicate that, within asingle run, smaller reasoning models achieve noticeable improvements in factual accuracy compared to their original instruction-tuned counterparts.
Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that adding test-time compute and token budgets factual accuracy consistently improves by 2–8%, further confirming the effectiveness of test-time scaling for enhancing performance and consequently improving reasoning accuracy in open-domain QA tasks. We release all the experimental artifacts for further research.

sections.1Introduction:
1
Introduction
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has highlighted the benefits of allocating additional computation at inference time, known as
test-time scaling
(Wu et al.,
2024
; Muennighoff et al.,
2025
; Zhang et al.,
2025
)
.
A straightforward method for leveraging this extra compute is to fine-tune models on datasets containing long chains of thought as a process with reflection, backtracking, and self-validation (i.e.,
thinking
), which has shown particular promise in mathematical reasoning tasks
Muennighoff et al. (
2025
)
.
In these settings, specialized reward models can verify intermediate steps
(Lightman et al.,
2023
; Wang et al.,
2024a
; Wu et al.,
2025b
)
. However, for complex
factual
tasks, it remains unclear whether longer reasoning processes lead to higher factual accuracy.
In this work, we address this gap by conducting large scale experiments for factual open-domain QA.
We extract reasoning traces from state-of-the-art reasoning models, namely
QwQ-32B
(Qwen Team,
2025
)
and
Deepseek-R1
(DeepSeek-AI,
2025
)
. To improve the accuracy and reliability of these traces, we additionally condition the two models with retrieved knowledge graph (KG) paths. KGs encode facts as directed, labeled graphs over entities and relations, and offer a structured foundation for verifying the validity of each reasoning step. We ground the questions from the
ComplexWebQuestions
dataset (CWQ;
Talmor and Berant,
2018
), QA benchmark constructed from complex SPARQL queries and human-paraphrased questions, with multi-hop KG paths from Wikidata
Vrandečić and Krötzsch (
2014
)
. We intend to introduce a verifiable fact-based scaffold to strengthen by introducing KG paths in the reasoning traces.
To study the effectiveness of long reasoning on the multi-hop QA task, we fine-tune six variants of the
Qwen2.5
architecture on both the original reasoning traces
(rt)
and the KG-enhanced traces, which we name fs1 and evaluate them across six benchmarks spanning a total

fs1: Enhancing Reasoning Traces with Knowledge Graphs
We attempt to steer the reasoning with KG paths to remove the inaccuracies in the reasoning traces. Since the CWQ dataset consists of entities from Freebase, we align them to their corresponding Wikidata entities. For each question in the dev. set of the CWQ dataset, relevant multi-hop KG paths are extracted from Wikidata using random walks using SPARQL queries as shown in
Appendix
F
. Each QA pair in the dataset may contain multiple valid KG paths, which are linearized graphs. We use the following prompt to obtain the improved reasoning traces: “
[Question]
\n\n
While answering the question, make use of the following linearised graph as an inspiration in your reasoning, not as the only answer:
\n\n
[KG Paths]
”. We do this with
QwQ-32B
and
Deepseek-R1

sections.4.2Budget Forcing: Does longer thinking:
4.2
Budget Forcing: Does longer thinking time induce better factuality in LLMs?
Following
Muennighoff et al. (
2025
)
, we investigate sequential scaling via interventions at decoding time that control the length of the model’s reasoning by imposing upper and/or lower bounds on the number of thinking tokens generated. To enforce a maximum length, we append the end-of-thinking delimiter (and optionally the phrase “Answer:”) to prompt the model to terminate its reasoning early and output its best available answer. Conversely, to impose a minimum reasoning length, we temporarily suppress the generation of the end-of-thinking delimiter and insert the prompt “Wait” to encourage continued reflection before providing a final answer. sections.5Related Work:
5
Related Work
5.1
Graph-enhanced In-context Learning
Recent efforts to enhance the factual consistency of LLMs using KGs have been explored in different directions. Semantic parsing methods
Lan and Jiang (
2020
); Ye et al. (
2021
)
convert natural language questions into formal KG queries; the retrieval-augmented method (KG-RAG)
Li et al. (
2023
); Sanmartin (
2024
); Jiang et al. (
2023
)
aims to reduce LLMs’ reliance on latent knowledge by incorporating explicit, structured information from KG; reasoning on graphs (RoG) model
Luo et al. (
2023
)
generates relation paths grounded
by KGs as faithful plans which are then used to retrieve valid reasoning paths from the KGs for LLMs to conduct faithful reasoning.
5.2
Long Form Factuality
Factuality in NLP involves multiple challenges
Augenstein et al. (
2024
)
. Several prior efforts explored factual reasoning, such as notably SAFE
Wei et al. (
2024b
)
and SimpleQA
Wei et al. (
2024a
)
. These datasets, however, despite accurate entities, lack explicit grounding in structured knowledge subgraphs. In contrast,
Tian et al. (
2024
)
directly address factual accuracy by fine-tuning models on automatically generated preference rankings prioritizing factual consistency.

sections.6Conclusion and Outlook:
6
Conclusion and Outlook
In this work, we have systematically investigated whether longer thinking, in the form of extended chain-of-thought reasoning, yields tangible gains in factual accuracy on complex open-domain QA tasks. By distilling more than 13K original and knowledge-graph-enhanced reasoning traces from state-of-the-art models (
QwQ-32B
and
Deepseek-R1
), constructing the fs1 corpus of 6K KG-grounded reasoning trajectories, and fine-tuning six instruction-tuned
Qwen2.5
variants across 168 experiments (totaling 1.7M traces) on six diverse benchmarks (22.6K questions), we have shown that smaller models (0.5–1.5B parameters) can indeed leverage longer, structured reasoning to improve single-run factual accuracy by up to 10 points over their instruction-tuned baselines. In contrast, models beyond 3B parameters exhibit less benefit from induced reasoning. Crucially, test-time scaling, whether via parallel repeated sampling or by expanding token budgets, consistently delivers 2-8 percent accuracy improvements even for our largest fine-tuned models, affirming the value of extra compute at inference for open-domain QA. By releasing all code, model checkpoints, and 1.7M reasoning traces (via both rt and fs1), we provide a rich resource for future work on process-level verification, hybrid scaling strategies, and the development of factuality-aware reward models capable of validating intermediate reasoning steps outside mathematical domains.
Limitations.
Our approach assumes that conditioning on a knowledge graph significantly improves the accuracy of reasoning traces, though it does not guarantee perfect outcomes. Additionally, accurately evaluating entity alignment poses challenges; we attempted to mitigate this limitation using LLM-based judgments and semantic similarity metrics, but these methods have their own inherent uncertainties.
